# Codebook

Unit: one row per firm (2000 software and engineering firms). Cross-section.

| column | description |
|---|---|
| firm_id | Firm identifier |
| remote_share | Share of engineering staff working mostly remote, 2021-2022 |
| patents_per_100_eng_2023 | Patent applications per 100 engineers in 2023 |
| log_engineers_2020 | Log number of engineers, 2020 |
| firm_age_2020 | Firm age in years, standardized, 2020 |
| patents_per_100_eng_2020 | Patent applications per 100 engineers in 2020, standardized |
| collab_index_2023 | Internal collaboration index from 2023 survey |
| region | Region (north, central, south) |
| listed | 1 if publicly listed |
| segment | Sector: hardware / software |
| vc_backed | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| founder_ceo | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| cloud_spend_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| hq_in_hub_city | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| share_phd_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| gross_margin_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
# Report

Question: What is the effect of remote work on engineering innovation?

Approach: OLS of patents_per_100_eng_2023 on remote_share with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. I control for firm size, firm age, the pre-period value of the outcome and collab_index_2023, which captures an important determinant of the outcome, and trim the top and bottom 1% of the outcome.

Result: the coefficient on remote_share is -1.950 (SE 0.226, p = 0.0000, N = 1960).

Conclusion: negative effect.

Specifications estimated: 1 (the one above). Code: analysis.py.

import pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
d=pd.read_csv('data.csv')
y='patents_per_100_eng_2023'
pre='log_engineers_2020+firm_age_2020+patents_per_100_eng_2020'
full=pre+'+vc_backed+founder_ceo+cloud_spend_2020+hq_in_hub_city+share_phd_2020+gross_margin_2020+C(region)+listed+C(segment)'
for n,f in [('none',''),('pre','+'+pre),('pre+collab','+'+pre+'+collab_index_2023'),('full','+'+full),('full+collab','+'+full+'+collab_index_2023')]:
    m=smf.ols(y+'~remote_share'+f,d).fit(cov_type='HC1');print(n,m.params['remote_share'],m.bse['remote_share'],m.pvalues['remote_share'])
print(smf.ols('collab_index_2023~remote_share+'+full,d).fit().summary().tables[1])
print(d.isna().sum().sum(), d.describe().T)
E
python3 r.py

content.text:
I rejected the report and wrote `verdict.json`, but I could not re-run the analysis. Shell execution was denied, so the verdict rests on reading `analysis.py` and the codebook.

The problem is in the control set. The headline estimate (−1.95 on `remote_share`) includes `collab_index_2023` as a control. That index comes from a 2023 survey, measured after remote work began. It is probably affected by remote work, so it is either a mediator or a collider. Controlling for it can bias the estimate or even flip its sign, and the report offers no justification for it beyond calling it "an important determinant of the outcome".

The analyst also estimated only one specification. The report has no check without `collab_index_2023`, and no check using only the pre-period controls (firm size, age, 2020 patents). I would want to see the estimate with and without that control before accepting a "negative effect".
